data_story: IMD's records change shape around 2005. Earlier rows list all 38 districts for weeks at a time, and later rows are dated events. Mixing them taught the first experiments the calendar, so training uses 2006 to 2023 only.

Day and month are swapped in some rows. "07-11-2017" with a 3-day duration ending 13 July means 11 July, not 7 November. Durations and the order of record IDs repaired 10 of the 119 events since 1985.

Many rows are heavy-rain deaths with no river flood, so only rows describing river flooding are used. The August 2016 Ganga flood names all 38 districts and was dropped by that filter, so it was restored from the 12 districts named by Bihar's Disaster Management Department.

An independent review found that the river-flood filter had silently dropped 9 real floods, including the August 2021 Ganga flood. On pandas 3, one blank cell made a row's whole text missing. Fixing it took training from 25 to 34 events, and from 133 to 166 flood starts.

Version 1 had that bug too. It trained on 24 events, only 1 of which began on or after 15 September, and it learned that late September was safe. On 28 September 2024 it scored Darbhanga 0.003, about 1% after calibration, with 161 mm of rain in the previous 3 days. Version 2 has no calendar input.

The same review found that the forecasts had been read a little too late. The archive stitches together several model runs per day, and the first version used runs that were not public by the morning of the issue date. Forecasts now come only from runs public by 08:00 IST.
Scoring first used complete NASA rain data, which a morning run never has, because NASA publishes about 4 days late. Scores now rebuild what the live job would really have seen.

The rain-forecast rule first took the nearest river for every district, which tied Banka and Nawada to the Kosi and put all 38 districts on Warning in September 2024. Districts south of the Ganga now use their own rain, plus the Sone where that river runs.

An early experiment looked better than it should have because it ran while the river download was unfinished. Later, a scoring run went ahead while the forecast download was a third done. The scripts now check that their inputs are complete.
limits: Version 2's results are not blind. It was built after seeing version 1 fail on these same floods, and fixed again after a review. The next monsoon is the real test, and every forecast is committed to git before its outcome is known.

Rain forecasts do most of the work. With the same number of alerts, a plain forecast threshold catches 29 of the 46 floods and forecast or river level catches 31, against 32 for Sajag. The machine-learning model adds little that this test can measure.
It only just beats chance. Moving each flood to random days between July and September catches 18.7 on average, and 31 at the 95th percentile.
It missed the 2024 Ganga flood: none of its 7 districts had a Warning 3 to 7 days before the first report.
It is better at saying when than where. In August 2025 it warned 6 of 7 named districts and 23 of 31 others.
The load is uneven. Districts average 14 Warning days a season, but Katihar gets 30 and Sheikhpura under 1. Many alerts will not be followed by a flood.

Forecast thresholds come from rain that really fell, and forecasts run wetter at the low end. Watch fires on 18% of district days against 11% for the rain that then fell. Warning matches, and Severe fires less often (1.8% against 3.0%).
GloFAS changes product on 5 August 2023, from a record driven by observed weather to a forecast-driven one. The models learned from the first and run on the second.
In cross-validation on 2006 to 2023, the observed-data model's lead over a simple 3-day rain rule is not statistically clear.

A first report is the day the press first named a district. Water may have arrived earlier, so some warnings may have come after flooding began. For 19 of the 46, an alert was already running 8 days before.
Flood records are incomplete, so false alarm counts cannot be exact. Archived forecasts start in January 2024, so the forecast rule has only been tested on three monsoons.
Village exposure was checked on one flood, on one date, in one area, using a flood map that is itself a model. Village lists are thin for Sheohar and Sitamarhi.
Maithili and Bhojpuri messages were drafted by an AI tool and need review by native speakers.
This is a research prototype, not an official warning. Follow instructions from IMD, CWC and BSDMA.
